title: Removing the 'my' from Autonomy
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien argues that the teacher-autonomy ideal of building everything from scratch is wasteful, using a Pad Thai analogy for the value of shared expertise and low variance. He cites the Grattan Institute's Ending the Lesson Lottery finding that top schools embed a collaboratively built, knowledge-rich curriculum and that teachers spend roughly six to ten hours a week creating resources. From experience, he describes a Year 7 team whose divergent resources pushed classes weeks apart, and his own clumsy phrase of going rogue that provoked a colleague to storm out. He explains resistance through the sunk-cost fallacy and says autonomy survives in delivery, anecdotes and attention cues. His advice to leaders is to honour past effort, model vulnerability and stress that students should not face a lesson lottery.
points: Grattan Institute research links high-performing schools to a shared, knowledge-rich, low-variance curriculum and shows teachers sinking hours into solo resource creation.
Divergent resources make assessment data meaningless and let timelines drift, as in a Year 7 team where classes ended up weeks apart.
Sunk-cost attachment explains why proposals for shared resources are heard as telling teachers their past work is worthless.
Autonomy remains in delivery, examples, think-alouds and routines, and shared planning also improves data analysis.
Change leaders should praise past effort, show vulnerability and keep the focus on removing the lottery for students.
quotes: Grattan’s report found that half of all teachers were planning on their own, that a typical teacher spent 6 hours per week creating resources and some teachers were spending up to 10 hours per week on resource creation.

What I chose to say was ‘we need to stop people going rogue in their classes as we cannot have assessments occurring months away from one another’. The words ‘going rogue’ did not go down well with many individuals and I fully admit it was a poor choice of words in my frustration with poor processes.
So when I come into a room and say ‘we all need to work together to create one central resource that everyone uses to best benefit the students learning’ obviously there is going to be pushback
Your autonomy comes from the way your present that resource to the class, the anecdotes you weave in, the way you break down your think alouds and worked examples.

If we do not acknowledge and praise the time and effort put in by teachers in the past we are going to be creating a true Sisyphean task for ourselves as we will be pushing an immovable boulder uphill for years to come.

We want students to know that it’s not a lottery which teacher they have in front of them because no matter who is teaching them they are teaching the same content in similar ways with the same resources and they have the exact same goal, to maximise the learning of students in their class.
